Editor’s Note: Thinking Out Loud

I started this section basically to write what the title says. A couple of
things I’ve been thinking deeply about in today's data engineering
landscape.

First, what makes a catalog truly open? Personally, I think the *Iceberg
catalog spec is the wrong step
https://example.com/link*;
it lets vendors build their own closed systems, limiting users' choices.

Second, do we still need to do data modeling? Years of designing and
building data platforms have taught me that frameworks serve an important
purpose: they give people a shared language for understanding complex ideas
and making decisions. A language transforms, *fades
https://example.com/link*,
and is *even born
https://example.com/link*;
data modeling is just a shared language. How will it evolve?

Share your thoughts on these two topics in the comments; I'd love to keep
the chat going.
------------------------------
Pinterest: Metrics Board: Building an Agent-ready Metrics Layer
https://example.com/link

Pinterest writes about the challenges with managing the metrics at scale,
and how scattered metric definitions and manual pipelines slowed
experiments and made reporting harder to trust. Metrics Board uses shared
metric definitions to automate calculation, quality checks, and publishing
across tools. Adoption of metric/ semantic layers is increasing across the
ecosystem.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Chenyu Zhang: The Semantic Layer Race: Snowflake, Databricks, Fabric IQ,
and Apache Ossie
https://example.com/link

As the need for and adoption of the headless semantic layer grows, it is no
surprise that all the major data platforms are offering it. The author
compares how Snowflake, Databricks, and Microsoft capture calculation rules
and business relationships, alongside Apache Ossie’s effort to exchange
definitions across tools. Reliable answers still require maintained rules,
clear ownership, and assistants that ask for clarification when several
meanings fit.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Event Alert: NEXT QUERY 2026 | Free Virtual Data + AI Summit | Nov 4
https://example.com/link

On November 4, NEXT QUERY 2026 brings those lessons into the open.
Engineers from Apple, NVIDIA, Coinbase, Intuit, AppLovin, Microsoft AI,
AWS, and Cisco will share what they built, what broke, and what they’d do
differently. Here’s some of what you’ll hear:

   -

   Coinbase and AppLovin share architecture lessons from production, and
   Intuit Mailchimp explains how it rebuilt its real-time customer data
   platform.
   -

   Get AWS’s take on running StarRocks on EKS, see how Apple runs analytics
   as a managed service, and hear how Carbon Arc moved 1 PB from Trino to
   StarRocks.
   -

   GPUs for analytics. NVIDIA explains why GPU execution is now practical
   for large-scale queries, and which workloads benefit most.

20+ talks across two tracks, hosted by PhoenixAI (the original creator of
StarRocks). Free and virtual, starting at 9:00 AM PT.

Can’t make it live? Register anyway, and we’ll send you the recordings
afterward.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
LinkedIn: Rebuilding LinkedIn’s Tracking Infrastructure: Scaling,
Migrating, and Hardening a High-Volume Event Pipeline
[image: Figure 1. Tracking events move from client SDKs through edge
routing and the ingestion service. Latency-sensitive signals follow a
direct real-time path, while Kafka supplies near-real-time and offline
processing.]
https://example.com/link

LinkedIn describes rebuilding its tracking pipeline where different event
types competed for the same resources. The approach essentially separated
workloads, removed repeated request data, and compared sampled outputs
while gradually moving traffic. The new service reached 90% of production
traffic with no migration-related incidents, highlighting the value of
verifying what downstream systems receive and keeping changes reversible.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Meta: Scaling AI-Native Analytics Patterns at Meta
https://example.com/link

Meta writes about how teams repeatedly rebuilt common measurements,
creating duplicate pipelines and inconsistent results. The article
describes how its Analytics Libraries generate pipelines from reusable
patterns, while agents use a tool that builds SQL from defined data models.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Microsoft: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data
visualizations
[image: Figure: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction
logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to
“what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the
heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which
makes interaction authoring more reliable and cost effective.]
https://example.com/link

Microsoft Research’s Flint-interactive evolves the declarative grammar
lineage pioneered by *Vega-Lite
https://example.com/link*
and *Mosaic
https://example.com/link*
for the agentic era, decoupling high-level semantic interaction specs from
low-level visual rendering to eliminate the token bloat and layout
fragility of LLM-generated charts. By pairing a state-machine compiler with
native MCP integration, it turns traditionally static AI charts into
bidirectional interfaces where user canvas selections feed directly back
into multi-turn conversational data workflows.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Snowflake: How we pushed CDC into Postgres, and turned replication into
clockwork
[image: Figure 1. Snowflake Postgres Data Mirroring]
https://example.com/link

Snowflake writes about challenges of keeping analytical copies of Postgres
data consistent as table structures change and failures occur. A Postgres
extension sends batches of changes through Iceberg tables, which Snowflake
applies while keeping related updates together. Queries can also include
pending changes, keeping results fresh even when destination tables are
updated less often.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
JioHotstar: The Kafka Optimization That Saved Us $350K a Year
https://example.com/link

JioHotstar writes about slashing Kafka infra cost by inserting a stateless
Go splitter service between their main ingestion topic and six downstream
consumers, scanning raw Protobuf wire tags and using a custom out-of-order
offset tracker to trim 7.5 KB client heartbeats down to 1.1 KB before
fan-out. The article is an excellent reminder of the importance of schema
design in event-stream architecture; if we get that wrong, we need a patch
like the one above to fix a schema design problem in the network layer.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
------------------------------
Meesho: Kafka at Meesho: How Meesho-Queue Made Kafka Simple at Scale
https://example.com/link

Meesho describes how inconsistent Kafka settings and applications tied to
specific clusters made tuning and migrations difficult. Meesho-Queue gives
applications a stable queue ID while centrally managing settings,
monitoring, and cluster assignments. This let the team move roughly 5,000
topics to its own Kafka infrastructure without requiring application code
changes.

*https://example.com/link
https://example.com/link*
